blocks.text: With regard to the human female, according to Midr. R. (Bereschit fol. 21, col. 1), the designation גברתא is said to be not in use. — גבר and דיכרי §. 151 denote the particular sexual maturity of the animal (Geiger: Zur Mischnah. 2nd part, p. 106). The name שכוי was a provincialism in the region of קן נשרייא (R. ha-Schana ad loc.); according to Jeruschalmi (Berachoth 13, c) that name was in use in רומי; cf. in general the cited passages of both Talmuds, which differ from each other extraordinarily in geographical respects.
Fürst derives the word from בִּרְבֵּר "to cry out," whence בִּרְבּוּר goose; others understand it to mean the swan; the Midr. R. (Kohelet fol, 88, col. 1)

The origin of moulting has not yet been sufficiently explained; like the shedding of skin in some amphibians, it is a process of rejection, and the new plumage a regeneration. — The Talmud in one passage (B. batra 73b) gives a reason, though it may not be applicable to all birds. It says there: We saw geese whose feathers fell out as a result of fatness. The fat then flowed out of the places in which the quills had sat. In fact most water birds, which as a rule are fatter than land birds, moult twice a year; most birds also moult in autumn, since they are then fatter than at any other season. However, swallows also moult, and indeed already in spring. In any case the moulting of fat birds can be explained by the fact that the fatness softens the skin and the quills lose their hold, whereby they fall out.

The spots are called: שורייקא סומקי, Raschi (Berachoth 7a): טייש Taches; on the other hand Raschi (Sanhedrin 105b) explains סורייקא by שורות שורות, lines, threads, and on A. Sara 4b Raschi uses the foreign word נוקיש and explains it as thread-like; he adds that in Arabic סוריאק, i.e., شِراك [shirāk], means thread.
However, all heavy birds have a longer lower leg; cf. Aristotle (Thierg. 2, 8, 3).

Striking is the error of Zipfer (L. Bl. d. Orients 1850, col. 310) that Agrippa sent gifts to the cock because he had heard its crowing at a distance of three parasangs (Joma 20b); there, however, it is not the cock that is meant but the crier Gebini, cf. Bartenoro on Tamid 3, 8. — Jerusalem Talmud Schekalim C. 5, H. 2 speaks not of three but of eight parasangs.
This and similar superstitions are most strictly forbidden by the rabbis; cf. my contribution: "Stimmen der Alten über und gegen den Aberglauben" in the "Jüdisches Volksblatt" vol. 1, p. 127 ff.
Elsewhere (Chulin 134b) ravens and bats are designated as those opposites, cf. §. 136.

Through the double treading of the cock it sometimes happens that an egg has two yolks; it is extremely rare, however, that inside the egg there is a second, fully formed one provided with a shell; I possess such a completely preserved egg, of the size of a swallow's egg, which I found in the white of a boiled hen's egg; it has the proper oval form and a pale white shell. It was located at the blunt end of the egg and was hard-boiled together with it.
Thus were named the bulls and sheep with whose breeding Pyrrhus occupied himself: Pyrrhic bulls, Pyrrhic sheep (Aristotle l. c. 3, 16, 7).

From this passage it follows that pigeons have a sense of smell, and this appears to be keenly developed, since it leads them onto the track of the decoy pigeon. Perhaps we might have here a hint toward the as yet unexplained phenomenon that pigeons return to their home from a distance of many miles in sure, direct flight. Thus pigeons had been carried in dark containers across the Channel from the English to the French coast, which then flew back and duly arrived at their former abode; smell perhaps appears to be the cause here.
Pekach b. Remaljahu is said (according to Midr. Jalk. Schim. 2nd part, fol. 133a) to have eaten 40, or even (ibid. fol. 138, c) 300 Sata of young pigeons as dessert.
On Raschi and his teachers cf. my נפשות צדיקים p. 101 ff.
In Maimuni (Introduction to the Order Seraïm. ed. Sulzbach 90a) one should read צפור דרור והוא הסנונית, not השממית.
R. ha-Schana 9b states: אין דרור אלא לשון חרות, "'דרור' has only the meaning: freedom."
L. Heller (on Negaim 14, 1), however, is of a different opinion, according to which the water was strongly coloured.

The passage (Chulin ibid.) reads: עוף המסרט כשר לטהרת מצורע "The bird that scratches is permitted to be taken as the purification offering of the leper." — Buxdorf committed the curious error of reading בשר "flesh," which is already false from the standpoint of natural history, since the swallow feeds only by snapping in the air, and thus never comes into a position to tear flesh with its claws.
Nempe avem סנונית aquilae esse terrori, quorsum Talmudici scripserint, valde obscurum est. Hirundinem ab aquila timeri naturae scrutatorum nullus observat.
The pl. of שליו is שְׁלָיִים (Jozar for Sabbat ha-Gadol s.v. אמיר), as in Num. 11, 31, where Jonathan has שלוי.
Partridges, it is true, build no nest, as already mentioned (§. 263), but scrape a spot into shape in a sunny place and then surround it with thorns and the like.

At 1. Sam. 26, 20 Raschi translates קורא as partridge, referring in this connection to Jerem. 17, 11; here, however, Raschi himself translates the word as: קוקו גלוצנט, Coucou gloussant. He also makes, on the first passage, the false statement that the קורא דגר (which here too undoubtedly denotes the cuckoo) broods the eggs of others, which, as mentioned (§. 264), is rather applicable to the partridge.
Bochart (Hieroz. 2, 2, 31, p. 344) reads in Raschi: שכבולה, vincta, bound, fastened.
